Scene · arrival

Quick printer help? :)

You’re the IT Support Manager. You’ve spent the last few months waking up, fixing problems, going home, and waiting until it’s reasonable to go to bed. Nothing is especially wrong. Nothing is especially interesting. You’ve reached the plateau, apparently, and the view is mostly emails and tickets.

Then a ticket pops up...

From: Daniel Hall, CEO
Subject: Quick printer help? :)

Hey! Having trouble getting the new printer working. Think it needs a driver? Whenever you have a minute. Appreciate you!

A printer driver. You hate those.

  • Head to his office. Maybe walking somewhere will count as feeling something.
  • Reply, “Have you tried restarting the printer?” You deserve to ask. Once.
  • Look up the printer’s model in inventory. There’s still a professional somewhere inside you.

Scene · office

Head to his office.

Forty-three seconds to Daniel’s office. His door is open, because his door is always open.

He looks up and his whole face reorganizes into welcome. “Hey! Gosh, thanks for coming down. Did you eat? I have a granola bar.”

You did eat. You decline. He apologizes for the ticket, for the printer, for having a printer at all.

There’s a Bible verse on a Post-it stuck to his monitor. A framed photo of his kids on the desk.

He offers you his chair. His phone lights up. “Sorry, gotta grab this. Holler if you need anything.” He steps out. The door doesn’t quite close.

You put your hands on the keyboard because your hands have to go somewhere.

You type your name. It’s a nothing keyboard, the kind companies buy in bulk for executives. You type your name again.

You’ve been typing on keyboards for twenty-two years. You have never noticed a keyboard before. You are noticing this keyboard.

You type a whole sentence: “Something is wrong with me.” You backspace it. The backspace also feels wonderful.

Daniel is still on the phone. Your hands are still on the keyboard.

  • Take it. Right now. You could be out of the building in ninety seconds. Probably.
  • Leave it. Come back for it later. You’d finish clean. You’d plan. That’s who you are.
  • Stand up. Walk away. Never think about this again. Everyone would tell you it’s the correct choice.
↑ Back to this box on the map

Scene · plan

The plan

You can’t stop thinking about the keyboard. Dinner, TV, the usual nothing. Except your fingers keep typing on the couch cushion.

You look it up. Full-size. Black and gray. $149.99. Four and a half stars. One reviewer wrote, “It’s a keyboard.” You buy one.

It arrives in a box big enough for a small pizza. You type your name at the kitchen table. Nothing. Same model, same clack. It has to be his. Some of his soul got into that one, or something. An x factor you cannot explain, and it draws you. Well. Now you have a decoy.

You’re early the next morning. You open a spreadsheet. Column A: Daniel’s schedule. Column B: Things that could go wrong. It’s the most alive you’ve felt in months, and it’s a crime. Or it will be.

IT can go anywhere. Nobody asks why. Daniel eats lunch at 12:15 and leaves his door open. Always. His assistant, Marcy, sits outside it and sees everything.

Over her shoulder, her calendar: the company retreat, next Friday. Daniel brings his own keyboard to every offsite. She calls it “the founding keyboard.” He started the company on it. Once it leaves the building, your chance is gone.

  • Case the office. Professionally. You are a professional.
  • Just ask him about it. Normal. He loves talking about his stuff.

Scene · outage

The outage

Daniel leaves for a meeting. His office is empty. You make it to the doorway. Marcy looks up. You crouch and examine a cable that doesn’t exist. “Everything okay?” “Cable.” She nods. Cables are a thing.

The next day, you take down the internet for “an emergency patch.” The building goes quiet, then loud. Ten people wander toward your desk holding their laptops like sick pets.

Marcy, who lives in her inbox, comes down herself. You tell her it’ll be back in two minutes. She thanks you. She goes to the break room for a snack.

You have two minutes. You walk into Daniel’s office. The keyboard is right there.

Next to it, on paper, because the internet is down: his retreat packing list. “Keyboard” is underlined twice.

He’ll pack it himself. If anything about it seems off, the first question will be who was in his office during the outage. That’s you.

  • Back out. Think. You can’t steal it from a cabin in the woods.

Scene · grandmother

The grandmother

You can’t steal it at the retreat. A cabin in the woods, forty coworkers, nowhere to hide. Once the keyboard leaves the building, it’s gone.

The retreat has to be canceled. You can’t cancel it. Daniel can.

Daniel hates leaving anyone out. Last year he canceled the retreat because one intern was allergic to the trees at the cabin.

All you need is a reason you can’t go. A sick relative. You have a mother in Ohio, who is fine and picks up her phone. Or you could hire a grandmother.

You post an ad: “Small family role. Elderly woman. $75/hour. No questions.” Three people reply. The first is a college student in a wig. They probably thought it was for a play. The second is a real grandmother, so old she doesn’t even know how to improvise a lie.

The third introduces herself as Mrs. Cox. She reads the brief, asks about your childhood, and tears up. You haven’t told her anything yet.

  • Hire Mrs. Cox. She’s far too good. That’s the point.
  • Forget it. Use your mother in Ohio. She’s fine. She picks up her phone. That may be a problem.
↑ Back to this box on the map

Scene · visit

The visit

You tell Daniel your grandmother is very sick and you can’t make the retreat. You look at the floor. You’re better at this than you should be.

He puts a hand over his heart. “Then we’re not going. Nobody gets left out.” Then he asks where she is. He’d like to visit.

Daniel arrives with flowers and a casserole. Mrs. Cox is propped up in a bed you rented by the hour. She knows your middle name. She knows your childhood dog’s name. You don’t remember telling her.

Daniel takes her hand and prays. She squeezes back. She’s crying real tears. “You’re a good grandkid,” she says to you. She means it more than you can bear.

He sends the email: “Family comes first. The retreat is canceled. Please keep our teammate’s grandmother in your prayers.” Marcy replies all with a heart. Forty people follow.

The email went out an hour ago. Mrs. Cox is still on the clock, and so is the bed. She’s holding Daniel’s hand, asking if he’s eating enough. He’s telling her about his kids.

  • Pay her and move on. Cash. No receipt.
  • Let Mrs. Cox keep going. She’s getting attached. So is he.

Scene · audit

The audit

You paid Mrs. Cox $150 in cash in a parking lot. She asked for a good review and left. The room cost almost as much. Add the decoy, and you’ve spent three keyboards’ worth of money to steal one keyboard.

Then, a new email, all staff: an asset audit. Every keyboard, every monitor, every stapler, scanned and logged.

Every keyboard is tagged. Your decoy isn’t. The moment anyone scans it, it’s over. You have exactly one day.

  • Make a tag. You’re in IT. You’re allowed a label printer.
  • Skip it. Nobody checks. Nobody ever checks. Probably.

Scene · swap

The swap

The supply closet. An asset tag is a barcode and a serial number. IT has the password to the asset list, so you look up Daniel’s keyboard and print its tag again, digit for digit. The night cleaner asks if you’re working late. “Inventory.” He does not ask about the barcode.

You’d swap them tonight, but security locks Daniel’s office at six, and it’s the one door IT doesn’t have a key to. It will have to be tomorrow, in the middle of the audit.

The auditor arrives at nine sharp with a scanner, a clipboard, and a face like an unopened envelope. He counts everything twice. He likes you. You’re the only one who answers his questions with numbers, which is worse.

You give him the tour, steering him away from Daniel’s office. He steers back. It is the last item on his list. You get there first.

The office is empty. The decoy goes on the desk. The real keyboard goes on the chair, for a second, while you straighten the cable. Footsteps. The auditor is in the doorway, scanner up.

He scans the keyboard on the desk. The forged tag beeps green. You have never been prouder of anything. “Well,” he says. He stops. He puts a hand to his chest. He starts to wheeze.

  • Look at him. Really look.

Scene · choice

The choice

He drops to one knee. His scanner clatters. He’s gasping like a man who’s run out of a word.

The keyboard is on the chair behind you. He’s on the floor now. For one second, you look at the keyboard.

You are shocked. Shocked that you looked at it at all. That it took you a whole second to look back at him. You feel guilty in a way you didn’t know you could.

You grab the keyboard and run anyway. Down the hall, past a fern and a poster that says TEAMWORK. Something skitters under your shoe. You look down. It’s an inhaler.

“Dang,” you say.

  • VIRTUE Go back with the inhaler. The keyboard is coming with you.
  • SIN Keep running. He can’t be that sick. Right?

Scene · lie

The lie

You slide back into the office on your knees. You press the inhaler into his hand. “You dropped this,” you say. “Ten seconds ago. I saw it.”

He breathes. He breathes again. He nods, eyes wet. He believes you completely.

He sits against the desk. He sees the keyboard in your arms. “Why did you grab the keyboard?” “I don’t know,” you say. “I wasn’t thinking about it. I just had it.”

It’s almost true. He decides what it means. “You grabbed what was in your hands and you came back,” he says, like he’s explaining you to yourself. He assumes you would never have let him die over a keyboard. That lands harder than the inhaler.

By evening, everyone knows about the inhaler. Nobody knows about the keyboard, which is in your bag. You should feel guilty. You do. You rationalize: the company wants happy employees. You are an employee. You are happy. Aren’t you?

Your phone buzzes. Daniel: “Heard what you did today. Thank you. You saved a man’s life.”

  • Go home. You’ve been waiting for this for weeks.

Real ending: The plateau · end_plateau

The plateau

You walk out with it in your bag. Past Marcy. Past the fern. Nobody stops you. Nobody checks. On Daniel’s desk, the decoy is already answering his emails. He hasn’t noticed. He never will.

At home, you take it out of the bag and set it on the kitchen table. You plug it in. Nobody is cheering. The refrigerator hums.

You type your name. It appears on the screen. It feels like a keyboard. It always did. What you felt in Daniel’s office was never the keyboard.

You wait for the rest of it. The part where it was worth it. You give it a minute. You give it a week.

That was the whole thing. That was all of it.

Nothing is especially wrong. Nothing is especially interesting. You’ve reached the plateau, apparently, and the view is mostly emails and tickets.

The end.

Scene · end_spare

Take it. Right now.

You pick it up. It weighs almost nothing. You walk out holding it in both hands, like a casserole.

Daniel is in the hallway, phone already lowered. “Oh! What are you doing with that?”

“It’s not working,” you say. “I’ll grab you a different one.”

“Oh no, that happened before!” He’s delighted to help. “Just unplug the little receiver and plug it back in. Don’t even need to reset anything.”

He does it for you, right there in the hallway. It works. Of course it works. “Honestly, keep it! I’ve got a spare in a drawer.” He holds it out to you with both hands.

It slips. It hits the floor. The space bar skates down the hall. Something inside makes a small, final sound.

Daniel looks at it. “Oh. Never mind. I’ll use the spare.”

You go back to your desk, where your emails and tickets are waiting.

You step away for coffee. When you come back, it’s on your desk, the space bar in a sandwich bag. A Post-it in Daniel’s handwriting: “Can you save him?”

You’re IT. Broken things come to you. You open it up. One spring, knocked loose. You put it back. You click the space bar on. You could tell Daniel it’s dead and keep it. Nobody would ever know.

You walk it back to his office instead. He plugs it in with a cable this time, “so he can’t get away again,” and offers you his chair to test it. You type your name. It still feels wonderful.

  • Go home. Try not to think about it. You will anyway.

Scene · end_mom

Forget it. Use your mother in Ohio.

You tell Daniel your mother is very sick. He is stricken. He is also thorough: he asks for her number, so he can pray with her.

She picks up on the first ring. She is fine. She is also confused. Daniel prays for three minutes. She says “Amen,” because she is polite.

She calls you back at six. “Who is Daniel and why is he so nice to me? Are you okay?”

She’s coming for a long visit. She has already booked the flight. The keyboard is still on Daniel’s desk.

Daniel tells you to take all the time you need. “Family comes first,” he says, with a hand over his heart.

  • Pick her up at the airport. She sounded worried. Not about herself.

Scene · Space · mom_lands

Pick her up at the airport.

Your mom comes through arrivals with one carry-on. She looks at you for about two seconds. “Oh, honey,” she says. “You’re bored.”

You tell her everything, right there by baggage claim: Daniel, the keyboard, the decoy, the grandmother you almost hired. She doesn’t look shocked. She looks interested.

“I’ve been bored since I retired,” she says. “Nothing’s especially wrong. Nothing’s especially interesting.” So it runs in the family.

The long visit lasts forty minutes. She has already bought you a seat on her flight home.

That night, in her kitchen in Ohio, she tells you about the moon rock at the Armstrong Air & Space Museum in Wapakoneta, half an hour away. A real piece of the Moon, from Apollo 11. She first saw it on a school trip when she was eight. She has wanted it ever since.

“You’ve got a plan for a keyboard,” she says. “Make one for a rock.”

  • Go in with a school field trip. Nobody counts the chaperones.
  • Go in at closing time. Your mom knows the guard. Your mom knows everybody.

Scene · Space · field_trip

Go in with a school field trip.

Your mom signs you both up to chaperone a fourth-grade field trip. Nobody checks. Nobody ever checks the chaperones.

Thirty kids hit the museum at once. One tries to climb into a space capsule. Two start crying. The guard runs toward the crying.

Your mom swaps the moon rock for a rock from her garden. Same size. Same gray. She practiced on the kitchen table. You know a decoy when you see one.

On the bus home, a fourth grader asks what’s in her purse. “A rock,” she says. It’s true.

  • Get it home. Act natural. You’re a chaperone.

Scene · Space · closing_time

Go in at closing time.

At 4:55 you’re in the museum, studying a spacesuit very hard. At five, the lights dim.

The guard knows your mom. She asks about his grandkids. He gets out his phone. She says “Oh, look at him” forty-one times.

You have the whole museum to yourself. You lift the glass. Somehow you thought the Moon would be heavier.

On the way out, your mom hugs the guard. He tells her to come back soon. She says she will. She probably will.

  • Get it home. Drive the speed limit. Exactly the speed limit.

Scene · Space · moon_rock

The rock

The moon rock sits on your mom’s kitchen table, next to the salt. You both look at it for a long time. “It’s a rock,” she says. You know this feeling. You paid $149.99 for it once.

On the TV in the next room, Artemis II launches from Florida in nine days: four astronauts, once around the Moon and home. The camera tours the capsule. Strapped to the wall with Velcro is a keyboard.

Everything NASA buys is the best one ever made, tested past the point of reason. That is the best keyboard on or off the planet.

Your mom turns the TV up. “They don’t keep the good stuff in Ohio,” she says, and drops the moon rock in her purse. It goes where she goes now.

You started with a CEO. Now it’s the government. Out of habit, you check the IT contract boards. Kennedy Space Center has posted a printer-driver ticket.

  • Take the printer-driver ticket. The task you hate most. Nobody on Earth wants it.
  • Hide in the cargo. Two crates marked “Crew supplies.” Close enough.

Scene · Space · printer_kennedy

Take the printer-driver ticket.

“Printer won’t print. Crew building. Urgent.” Every IT person in Florida has scrolled past it. You take it. You fly down with your mom, who is listed as your assistant and has packed sandwiches.

It’s the worst printer driver you have ever installed. It takes four hours. For the first time in your career, you don’t hate it.

The printer prints the crew’s checklists. Everyone thanks you. Nobody takes back your badge.

IT can go anywhere. Nobody asks why. Not even at NASA. On launch morning, nobody asks why you and your mom are in the capsule, either.

  • Find somewhere to hide. Behind the seats. Very still. Very small.
↑ Back to this box on the map

Scene · Space · crew_supplies

Hide in the cargo.

Two crates are marked “Crew supplies.” You and your mom are crew supplies now. She packs sandwiches.

A forklift lifts you. A truck drives you somewhere flat and hot. An elevator goes up for a very long time.

Hours later, you lift the lid an inch. You’re inside the capsule. Next to you, your mom’s lid lifts an inch too.

Four astronauts climb in and strap down. Nobody checks the crew supplies. Somewhere far below, someone starts a countdown.

  • Stay very still. You’re crew supplies. Act like it.

Scene · Space · liftoff

Liftoff

Zero. The whole world shakes for eight minutes. Somewhere in the dark, your mom finds your hand and holds it the entire time. You haven’t held her hand since you were nine.

Then it goes quiet. A pen floats past your face. Then one of your mom’s sandwiches.

The astronauts find you about an hour later. There’s a lot of language. The commander calls Houston, and Houston is quiet for a very long time.

You can’t turn a moon rocket around. They give you a corner, two straps and one rule: don’t touch anything.

It takes five days to reach the Moon. The keyboard is on the wall the whole way, six feet from you.

  • Wait until they sleep. Even astronauts sleep. Eventually.
  • Let your mom distract them. She has questions. So many questions.

Scene · Space · lights_out

Wait until they sleep.

Astronauts sleep in bags strapped to the walls. You wait until all four are breathing slowly. Your mom gives you a thumbs-up.

You push off toward the keyboard. You push off a little too hard.

You sail past it, spin, and kick something behind a panel. It makes a noise like a blender eating a spoon. Then it makes no noise at all.

You peel the keyboard off the wall. Velcro is very loud at night. The lights come on.

  • Hide it behind your back. In a capsule this small.

Scene · Space · mom_tour

Let your mom distract them.

Your mom has questions. How do you sleep? How do you eat? How does the bathroom work?

The astronauts are polite, because she is. They give her a tour of the toilet. She asks what one button does. All four of them say “Don’t.”

She has already pressed it. The toilet makes a noise like a blender eating a spoon. Then it makes no noise at all.

While everyone stares at the toilet, you peel the keyboard off the wall. Velcro is very loud. Nobody hears it.

  • Hide it behind your back. Act casual. In zero gravity.

Scene · Space · toilet

The toilet

The toilet is broken. It cost twenty-three million dollars. Its fan is jammed. Nobody says whose fault it is. Nobody has to.

Houston says it will still take one kind of business. Not the other kind. Four astronauts look at you. It’s a long way home.

The keyboard is behind your back. Your mom is looking at a small hatch you never noticed before. A label on it says ESCAPE POD. It isn’t in any of the brochures.

You’re IT. Broken things come to you.

  • Grab your mom. Take the escape pod. Keyboard and all. Somebody else can fix the toilet.
  • Put the keyboard back. Fix the toilet. It’s a ticket. You know what to do with tickets.

Scene · Space · escape_pod

Grab your mom. Take the escape pod.

The escape pod has two seats, one parachute and no instructions.

Your mom leaves the moon rock on the commander’s seat with a note: “Sorry about the toilet.” It’s closer to home up here anyway. Then she climbs in.

The pod swings once around the Moon and falls toward Earth. The keyboard is in your lap. Your mom is laughing. You realize you are too.

Three days later, you splash down in Lake Erie. A fishing boat picks you up. The captain doesn’t ask. Ohio doesn’t ask.

  • Take it home. The keyboard. And your mom.

Real ending: A little spice · Space · spice

Take it home.

Your mom’s computer is older than some of your coworkers. The keyboard that went around the Moon plugs right in.

She types her bingo newsletter on it. You type your name. It feels wonderful. You’re pretty sure it isn’t the keyboard.

She reads the newsletter out loud, doing voices. You laugh until you have to sit on the floor. The refrigerator hums. Nobody minds.

Daniel texts to ask how your mother is doing. “Better,” you write back. “So am I.”

You didn’t need a keyboard. You needed a little spice.

The end.

Real ending: The far side · Space · far_side

Put the keyboard back. Fix the toilet.

You Velcro the keyboard back to the wall. Then you take the panel off the toilet.

Houston talks you through it. Something small is jammed in the fan. You don’t ask what. You get it out. The fan spins. Nobody shakes your hand. Everybody thanks you.

That night, Orion swings behind the Moon. There’s no signal back there. No Houston. No Daniel. No emails. No tickets.

Your mom holds the moon rock up to the window, right next to the Moon. “Look,” she says. “It’s home.”

Nothing is especially wrong. Everything is especially interesting.

The end.

Dead end: Method · end_method

Let Mrs. Cox keep going.

You let Mrs. Cox keep going. She is not a woman who stops. She tells Daniel he reminds her of her late husband, Walter.

By Friday, Daniel has given her the guest room. By Monday, she is at the all-hands, taking notes.

She catches your eye across the conference table and mouths: “You owe me.” She is not wrong.

She’s at Daniel’s side every day now. Nobody knows she’s hired help except you. You never get near the keyboard again.

Dead end: Asset not found · end_red

Skip it. Nobody checks.

You skip the tag. You do the swap at lunch. Nobody checks, you tell yourself.

The auditor checks. He scans the keyboard on Daniel’s desk. It beeps once. Red. “Asset not found,” says the scanner, very calmly.

He looks at the keyboard. He looks at you. He has seen this before, and he is sad about it. He calls Daniel in.

Daniel arrives holding a granola bar. He looks at the keyboard, then at you. He is heartbroken. “I would’ve just given it to you.” You are asked to leave. The real keyboard was in your bag the whole time. It feels like nothing.

Scene · Hell · end_running

Keep running.

You keep running. Past Marcy and her granola bar. Down the stairs: lobby, basement, B2, which the building doesn’t have. B9. It gets warm. Then very warm.

At the bottom, a sign: WELCOME TO HELL, PLEASE TAKE A NUMBER. A demon at the front desk prints you a lanyard. “You’re early. Most people die first. The auditor will be fine, by the way. You didn’t know that when you ran.”

“Bring the keyboard. Orientation is at nine. And yes, the running is already on your record.”

  • SIN Sign in. Keep the keyboard. Everyone brings something. You brought someone else’s.
  • VIRTUE Run back up and face it. Up has to be somewhere. So does everything you ran from.

Real ending: Not the hero · Hell · hell_upstairs

Run back up and face it.

You run back up, past the B2 that doesn’t exist, and come out by the fern at 8:59 the next morning. The auditor is fine. He’s also very clear about who ran.

HR is waiting. Daniel looks so disappointed you almost feel something. Security takes the keyboard and walks you out.

You went back to face it. You’re just a day late, and nobody up here gives points for that.

The end.

Scene · Hell · hell_orientation

Orientation

Orientation: no windows, a hum someone chose on purpose, deviled eggs. Compliance counts the chairs twice and opens a file with your name on it.

The demon who brought the eggs is so happy you’re here their tail wags. The nicest demon in Hell, everyone says, a little tiredly. They hand you their pitchfork to “get a feel for it” during the safety video.

The handle is warm. The balance is perfect. You poke the air, and the air seems grateful. The keyboard under your other arm feels like nothing now. Uh oh.

  • VIRTUE Hand it back. Smile. It isn’t yours.

The corner office

He scrolls through your soul for a long time. “It’s mostly emails and tickets,” he says, not unkindly. His eyes drift to the keyboard under your arm.

Real ending: Driver unavailable · Hell · hell_job

Sell him Daniel’s keyboard.

The Devil types his name on Daniel’s keyboard. Then again. “Oh,” he says. “Oh, I see.” He signs before you can change your mind.

A pitchfork given for keeps comes with its owner’s job. It’s in the bylaws. A headset arrives from Ohio with a note: “Gosh! First vacation since the Bronze Age!”

Your desk faces a wall of monitors. On every one, an IT Support Manager is reading “Driver unavailable.” You tap a key with the pitchfork. A printer in Tulsa stops working.

You hate printer drivers, and you are extraordinary at this. You just weren’t expecting to do it for the rest of your life.

The end.

Real ending: The lower plateau · Hell · hell_plateau

The lower plateau

One good deed, a little late. Down here, that counts for exactly nothing. Nobody is cheering. The Lake of Fire hums.

You get a cubicle and a lot of Tuesdays. Somewhere, a pitchfork leans against a wall. It feels like a pitchfork. It always did. What you felt at orientation was never the pitchfork.

Real ending: Eleven years · end_wizard

Ask him to show you.

He holds out his hand for the decoy in your bag. He knew about it the whole time. He taps it twice and hands it back.

That’s the whole spell. No chanting. Nothing catches fire.

That night your keyboard types on its own. In the morning there’s money in an account you never opened, from a company that doesn’t exist.

You never fix another printer. You never open another ticket. You wake up with nothing to do and nothing wrong, and you smile the way Daniel smiles.

Danal hasn’t felt a single thing in centuries. He’s never noticed.

Neither will you.

The end.
